statement: Different whole numbers are chosen from 1 to 30. What is the least number that must be chosen to be certain that two of the chosen numbers add up to a multiple of 7?

choices.misconception: I put the remainders into four boxes, {0}, {1, 6}, {2, 5} and {3, 4}, and took one more than the number of boxes.
I took one more than the seven possible remainders, as if two numbers with the same remainder always worked.
I assumed every remainder appears exactly 4 times, so I found a safe set of 1 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 13 and added one.
I found the largest safe set, 15 numbers, and reported its size instead of one more.

hints: Sort the numbers by their remainder on division by 7.
Two numbers add to a multiple of 7 when their remainders are 0 and 0, 1 and 6, 2 and 5, or 3 and 4. Build the largest set avoiding these, then add one. The remainder classes differ in size.
Remainders 1 and 2 each have 5 numbers from 1 to 30; every other remainder has 4. A safe set takes at most one multiple of 7 and the larger class from each pair.

solutions.reliable: From 1 to 30, the remainders 1 and 2 on division by 7 each occur 5 times (1, 8, 15, 22, 29 and 2, 9, 16, 23, 30) and the other five remainders occur 4 times each. Two chosen numbers add to a multiple of 7 exactly when their remainders are 0 and 0, 1 and 6, 2 and 5, or 3 and 4. A safe set can hold at most one multiple of 7, and from each pair of classes only one class: the best is all of class 1 (5 numbers), all of class 2 (5) and all of class 3 or class 4 (4). That is 1 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 15 numbers, for example 7, 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, 2, 9, 16, 23, 30, 3, 10, 17, 24. So 15 numbers can avoid it and 16 cannot. The transferable idea: in a pigeonhole problem, build the largest set that avoids the event; the answer is one more than its size.

whyOnTest: Pigeonhole questions with sums test building the right boxes and the largest safe set, and here also counting classes of unequal size rather than assuming they are equal.
